problem: Existing ObjectNav methods assume a closed vocabulary of object categories. They rely on annotated 3D scans, category-specific detectors or segmenters, and ObjectNav rewards or human demonstrations. Prior zero-shot attempts are weak: ZER (11.3% SR on Gibson) is still closed-set, and CoW (11.1% SR on MP3D) uses a heuristic, non-learned exploration policy.
motivation: A home robot should find objects described in free-form language ('bathroom sink', 'flat-head screwdriver'), yet collecting ObjectNav annotations and demonstrations is costly and limits scale. ImageNav episodes can be generated procedurally in any unannotated scene. CLIP maps images and text into a shared semantic space, so a CLIP image embedding of a goal photo should resemble the CLIP text embedding of the same target. That makes the two modalities interchangeable as navigation goals.
key_idea: Train an RL navigation agent on ImageNav at scale (800 unannotated HM3D scenes), with goal images encoded by frozen CLIP's image encoder into a semantic-goal space. At test time, swap in CLIP's text encoder so the same policy performs open-vocabulary ObjectNav zero-shot.
insight: Decoupling goal representation (a pretrained, semantics-by-design CLIP space) from learning to navigate lets cheap image-goal data teach semantic navigation. At a matched setup (ResNet-9, Gibson training, no pretraining; Table 2) this beats ZER's reverse design of learning image embeddings from scratch and then mapping categories in: 15.3 vs 11.3 ObjectNav SR. The ablations show that what matters for zero-shot transfer differs from what matters for the training task. OVRL visual-encoder pretraining raises ImageNav SR by only 4.5-5.8 points but ObjectNav SR by 9.4-10.4 (Table 3). Scaling from 72 Gibson to 800 HM3D scenes slightly lowers ImageNav SR (-0.9) but raises ObjectNav SR by 6.6 (31.3 vs 24.7). A larger ResNet-50 trained from scratch is worse than ResNet-9 from scratch (16.6 vs 20.9 ObjectNav SR; Table 6), so extra capacity helps only when it is pretrained.
method: Semantic-goal embedding: goal images are pre-encoded offline with the frozen CLIP ResNet-50 image encoder into 1024-d vectors s_g = CLIP_v(v_g). This also speeds up training by about 3.5x.

SemanticNav agent: the egocentric RGB frame is encoded by a ResNet-50 pretrained with DINO self-supervision on the Omnidata Starter Dataset (OVRL recipe). Its output is concatenated with the goal embedding and a previous-action embedding, then fed to a 2-layer LSTM policy that outputs a distribution over 4 discrete actions.

Large-scale ImageNav training data: 9k episodes per scene (EASY 1.5-3 m / MEDIUM 3-5 m / HARD 5-10 m) over 800 HM3D train scenes gives 7.2M episodes. Goal images are sampled at 4 heading angles, for 36M episodes (as printed). Separate datasets are built for agent configuration A (ImageNav-style, 1.5 m tall, 128x128 RGB, 90° HFOV) and configuration B (LoCoBot-like, 0.88 m tall, 640x480 RGB, 79° HFOV).

RL training: DD-PPO for 500M steps on 8 A40 GPUs (about 1,704 GPU-hours for two agents), with color-jitter and random-translation augmentation. The reward follows ZER: r = r_success(5) + r_angle-success(5, if within 25° of the goal heading) − Δdistance-to-goal − Δangle-to-goal (angle term only within 1 m) − 0.01 slack, which pushes the agent to face the goal before STOP.

Zero-shot ObjectNav transfer: the category name (e.g., 'sofa', no prompt template) is encoded with the CLIP text encoder, s_g = CLIP_t(o_g), and plugged into the same policy. Free-form goals like 'kitchen sink' or 'sink and a stove' also work.
Optional fine-tuning (Appendix B, not zero-shot): the ImageNav-trained agent is further RL-fine-tuned on annotated MP3D (25M steps) or HM3D (100M steps) ObjectNav data.

setting.training_data: ImageNav episodes auto-generated in 800 unannotated HM3D train scenes: 7.2M episodes, 36M after 4-heading goal augmentation, 500M DD-PPO steps. Encoder pretrained with DINO on the Omnidata Starter Dataset; CLIP pretrained on 400M image-text pairs. No ObjectNav annotations or demonstrations (fine-tuned variants additionally use ObjectNav RL on MP3D/HM3D).
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB (no depth, no GPS/compass) + goal embedding (CLIP image embedding for ImageNav, CLIP text embedding for ObjectNav)
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN_LEFT/RIGHT 30°, STOP

numbers_note: All results are on validation splits (no test-standard). The best checkpoint was selected by ObjectNav validation SR, i.e. on the same split that is reported. Results are averaged over 3 evaluation runs (SR std: 0.02% Gibson, 0.46% HM3D, 0.11% MP3D). Open-world and compound-instruction results ('bathroom sink', 'sink and a stove') are qualitative only, shown in figures. Table 6 adds a ResNet-50-from-scratch HM3D variant (Gibson ObjectNav SPL 6.9 / SR 16.6) and Table 3 row 2 a ResNet-9-from-scratch HM3D variant (SPL 9.5 / SR 20.9); neither is listed above.
results: Zero-shot ZSON reaches 31.3% SR on Gibson ObjectNav vs 11.3% for ZER (+20.0). On MP3D it reaches 15.3% SR vs 11.1% for CoW, which uses depth (+4.2), though its SPL is 1.5 points lower (4.8 vs 6.3). On HM3D it gets 25.5% SR / 12.6% SPL, and this SPL matches the fully supervised OVRL (12.3%) trained on 40k human demonstrations. It also beats ZER on Gibson ImageNav (36.9 vs 29.2 SR). Fine-tuning ZSON with ObjectNav RL raises HM3D to 49.6% SR / 27.0% SPL and MP3D to 22.9% SR / 9.2% SPL.
limitations: The agent learns dataset priors (e.g., stoves are in kitchens), so it may fail when targets are in unusual locations, and training-scene biases may affect deployment.

Observed failure modes include poor exploration (never entering the target room), stopping short, and confusing look-alike objects (desk vs table, dresser vs cabinet). SPL remains low, below CoW's on MP3D.
Evaluation is simulation only. Open-world ability is shown only qualitatively. Checkpoints are selected on the reported ObjectNav validation split, and two agents cost about 1,704 GPU-hours.
